terms.gloss: costume, get-up: the dress of a part
evidence: Plaut. Mil. 1177: facitō utī veniās ōrnātū hūc ad nōs nauclēricō
Plaut. Trin. 1099: quis iste est tuos ōrnātus?
terms.comment: Plautus’s word for the dress in which someone plays a part: ōrnātū nauclēricō, dressed as a ship’s captain; ōrnātum capere, to put on one’s costume. So “dress up as a knight” is equitis ōrnātum capere or ōrnātū equitis venīre; for the knight, eques (Morgan–Owens).

phrases.english: Why are you all dressed up?

phrases.latin: Equitis ōrnātum capiam: dā mihi galeam et gladium ligneum.
phrases.english: I’ll dress up as a knight: give me a helmet and a wooden sword.

phrases.latin: facitō utī veniās ōrnātū hūc ad nōs nauclēricō … adsimulātō quasi gubernātor siēs
phrases.english: mind you come here to us dressed up as a ship’s captain … pretend you’re a helmsman

phrases.latin: sed quis iste est tuos ōrnātus?
phrases.english: but what’s that get-up of yours?

sources: Lewis & Short: exorno · Lewis & Short: suborno · Lewis & Short: ornatus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 96, 116, 302, 306.
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. knight.
